summary:
Kirov Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia in full. The sources reviewed identify no deviation in this oblast material enough to assess separately, so the national position applies here without local modification and the national score is adopted for this record.

Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are both banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.

The 2013 "gay propaganda" law carries administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, rising to as much as four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Since the Supreme Court's 2023 extremist designation of the international LGBT+ movement, participation in it carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years.

Foreigners found guilty of violating the propaganda law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and then deported, and displaying certain symbols, including the rainbow flag, is a crime. The US State Department advises against all travel to Russia on this basis.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, approximately 98 administrative and three criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its symbols. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, among them three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The UK Home Office assesses that openly LGBT+ people in Russia face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them, and records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024. LGBT+ people are treated as a particular social group under the refugee convention for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement wave documented nationally has an administrative as well as a criminal face: of the 101 extremism-related convictions recorded by Human Rights Watch by 30 June 2025, roughly 98 were administrative and only three criminal, so the bulk of cases produce fines and records rather than prison terms. Criminal exposure concentrates in the more serious charges, with organising under the designation carrying six to ten years and article 282.2 charges against publishing-house staff carrying up to 12 years.

Two foreign governments have put the risk on record. The US State Department advises against all travel to Russia and specifies the arrest, short detention and deportation sequence for foreigners who violate the propaganda law, while the UK Home Office country policy note sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims and finds the state able but unwilling to protect LGBT+ people.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kirov Oblast live under the same national prohibitions as visitors, with no oblast-level relief identified: gender-marker changes are unavailable, legal gender recognition is banned, and trans-specific healthcare has been effectively unavailable since 2023.

The UK Home Office records at least 139 people across Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may reach the level of persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them. For residents, unlike visitors, the pathway out of that exposure is an asylum claim abroad rather than short-term detention and removal.

Displaying banned symbols is the most common route into the case system for residents: 81 people were convicted across 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 between January 2024 and June 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Kirov Oblast-specific enforcement data appears in the inventory. The number of extremism or propaganda cases opened in this oblast, the courts that hear them and any local raids or detentions are not sourced, and nothing here should be read as evidence that enforcement in Kirov Oblast is lighter or heavier than the national pattern.

The oblast-level position on facilities, police conduct toward trans residents, and access to documentation procedures is unresolved in these sources; the summary rests on the absence of identified regional deviation rather than on positive local findings.

The count of at least 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 comes from the UK Home Office note and its methodology, including what counts as an impacted person, is not detailed in the inventory.
